games.title: Yie Ar Kung-Fu
games.note: Introduced health meters and a run of opponents with different fighting styles and weapons.

games.title: International Karate
games.note: Published in the US by Epyx as World Karate Championship.

games.title: Fatal Fury
games.note: Fighters could jump between two planes of the stage. It introduced Terry Bogard.

games.title: Art of Fighting
games.note: Wikipedia credits it with originating taunts in fighting games; the camera zoomed in on its large fighters.

games.title: The King of Fighters '94
games.note: Introduced three-on-three team battles; its prototype was a side-scrolling beat 'em up called Survivor.

games.title: Garou: Mark of the Wolves
games.note: The last Fatal Fury until 2025; Terry Bogard is the only returning fighter.

games.title: Samurai Shodown
games.note: SNK's first weapon-based fighting game, set in feudal Japan; it began as a planned side-scrolling beat 'em up.

games.title: Street Fighter III
games.note: Subtitled New Generation; it replaced almost the whole cast and added parrying.

games.title: Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike
games.note: Famous for 'Evo Moment 37', Daigo Umehara's run of parries at Evo 2004.

games.title: Mortal Kombat (2011)
games.note: NetherRealm was formed from Midway's Chicago studio, the original Mortal Kombat team.

games.title: Mortal Kombat 1
games.note: Restarted the timeline after Liu Kang became the Fire God at the end of Mortal Kombat 11.

games.title: Injustice: Gods Among Us
games.note: DC Comics heroes hurl cars and smash each other through walls into new parts of a stage.

games.title: Virtua Fighter
games.note: The first fighting game with 3D polygon characters. John Romero and Toby Gard both named it as an influence.

games.title: Dead or Alive
games.note: Ran on Sega's Model 2 arcade board, the same one used by Virtua Fighter 2.

games.title: Tekken 8
games.note: Added the Heat system, which rewards aggressive play.

games.title: Soul Edge
games.note: Released on PlayStation outside Japan as Soul Blade.

games.title: Soulcalibur
games.note: Its Dreamcast port was a North American launch title in 1999.

games.title: Killer Instinct
games.note: Published by Midway in arcades; built around long automatic combos and 'combo breakers'.

games.title: Darkstalkers
games.note: Known in Japan as Vampire; its cast of classic monsters includes a vampire, a werewolf and a succubus.

games.title: X-Men vs. Street Fighter
games.note: An early tag-team fighting game, where players switch between two characters mid-fight.

games.title: Marvel vs. Capcom
games.note: Mega Man and Strider meet Spider-Man and Wolverine, with guest characters called in for single assists.

games.title: Marvel vs. Capcom 2
games.note: Three-on-three tag battles with a cast of 56 fighters.

games.title: Guilty Gear
games.note: Daisuke Ishiwatari designed the characters, wrote the story and composed its rock and metal music.

games.title: Guilty Gear Strive
games.note: Uses 3D models shaded and animated to look like hand-drawn 2D art.

games.title: BlazBlue: Calamity Trigger
games.note: Each character has a unique 'Drive' mechanic.

games.title: Dragon Ball FighterZ
games.note: Producer Tomoko Hiroki explained its three-person teams: it 'would feel a bit odd' to see Goku defeated by Krillin.

games.title: Granblue Fantasy Versus
games.note: Based on Cygames' mobile RPG, with optional one-button special moves.

games.title: Brawlhalla
games.note: A free-to-play platform fighter; Ubisoft bought the studio in 2018.

games.title: Rivals of Aether
games.note: A spiritual sequel to Super Smash Land, Dan Fornace's fan-made demake of Super Smash Bros.

games.title: MultiVersus
games.note: Warner Bros. characters like Bugs Bunny and Batman; relaunched in 2024, its servers closed in May 2025.

games.title: Nickelodeon All-Star Brawl
games.note: SpongeBob, the Ninja Turtles and other Nickelodeon characters in a platform fighter.

games.title: The Outfoxies
games.note: Rival assassins fight with guns and grabbed items through moving, multi-level stages.

games.title: Ikari Warriors
games.note: Two commandos fight up a scrolling battlefield, aiming with rotary joysticks.

games.title: Skullgirls
games.note: Mike Zaimont was building a fighting game engine in his spare time when he met artist Alex Ahad.

links.took: One-on-one martial arts duels, the format Karate Champ established.
links.added: A series of opponents with different styles and weapons, and health meters.

links.took: Karate Champ's two-fighter karate bouts, refereed and scored in points.
links.added: Backdrops from around the world and smoother animation on home computers.
links.extra: Data East sued, calling it a copy; the appeals court ruled for Epyx in 1988, finding it similar but not identical.

links.took: Its boss fights: Takashi Nishiyama considered making a whole game around them.
links.added: Head-to-head bouts against martial artists from around the world, with pressure-sensitive punch pads.

src.t: Wikipedia: Street Fighter (cites a Polygon oral history)

links.took: One-on-one martial arts bouts, part of Street Fighter's basic template.
links.added: Special moves performed with joystick motions, and blocking.
links.extra: Wikipedia names Karate Champ, Kung-Fu Master and Yie Ar Kung-Fu as its basic template.

links.took: Health meters and a run of opponents with different styles.
links.added: Ryu and Ken, stages around the world and secret special moves.

links.took: Karate Champ's style of bout; Tobias and Boon first imagined one with large digitized characters.
links.added: Digitized actors, gore and secret finishing moves.

src.t: Wikipedia: Mortal Kombat (1992), citing John Tobias

links.took: Its dizzy state, which Ed Boon turned into finishing moves, and the arcade boom SF2 created.
links.added: Fatalities: gruesome finishers performed after the fight is won, plus digitized actors.
links.extra: Boon and Tobias read Midway's brief as a fighting game to compete with Street Fighter II.

links.took: The Final Fight team, which went on to make Street Fighter II.
links.added: Eight playable world warriors with their own special moves, and combos.

links.took: Street Fighter's one-on-one design; Takashi Nishiyama envisioned Fatal Fury as its spiritual successor.
links.added: Two stage planes to jump between, and a story about Terry Bogard and Geese Howard.
links.extra: Fatal Fury was developed around the same time as Street Fighter II.

links.took: SNK's fighting-game team and the South Town setting.
links.added: Zooming sprites, a spirit gauge for special moves, and taunts that drain it.

links.took: Fighters from Fatal Fury, such as Terry Bogard.
links.added: Three-on-three team battles mixing several SNK casts.

links.took: Art of Fighting's cast, including Ryo Sakazaki.
links.added: A crossover tournament with teams from several SNK series.

links.took: Ikari Warriors' commando heroes, updated as KOF's Ikari team.
links.added: Soldiers recast as fighters in a three-on-three tournament.

links.took: Its prototype was a Double Dragon-style side-scrolling beat 'em up called Survivor.
links.added: Kept only Survivor's three-person teams, turning them into three-on-three fights.

links.took: Fatal Fury's South Town and Terry Bogard.
links.added: A new generation of fighters led by Rock Howard, and 'Just Defend' blocking.

links.took: Street Fighter II standardized the one-on-one fighting game.
links.added: Swords and other weapons, feudal Japan, and heavy damage from single hits.

links.took: Street Fighter II standardized the one-on-one fighting game.
links.added: 3D polygon fighters and a simple guard, punch and kick layout.

links.took: Samurai Shodown popularized weapon-based one-on-one fighting.
links.added: 3D weapon duels, weapons that can break, and ring-outs.

links.took: Namco's 3D weapon-fighting series and its cast.
links.added: The 8-Way Run for free movement around the arena.

links.took: Close work with Namco's Tekken team, with Tekken 3 used as a reference for movement.
links.added: Weapon-based fighters and full eight-way movement.

links.took: Street Fighter's attack set of punches and kicks.
links.added: Automatic combos, 'combo breakers' and pre-rendered 3D-look fighters.

links.took: Mortal Kombat's finishing moves.
links.added: Ultra combos and 'No Mercy' finishers in a combo-focused fighting game.
links.extra: Rare was planning to rival the success of Mortal Kombat.

links.took: Ideas from SNK's Fatal Fury and World Heroes, which Nintendo's Ken Lobb named as influences.
links.added: Rare's pre-rendered graphics and a combo system built around breakers.

src.t: Ken Lobb (Nintendo), in Wikipedia: Killer Instinct (1994)

links.took: Capcom's fighting-game know-how from Street Fighter II.
links.added: A monster cast, chain combos and blocking in mid-air.

links.took: Alex Ahad's art style and character designs drew on Darkstalkers.
links.added: Hand-drawn fighters with a dark 1940s look.

links.took: Tag teams, assists and a control scheme modeled on Marvel vs. Capcom 2.
links.added: Teams of one to three fighters with balanced health, and protection against infinite combos.

links.took: Street Fighter II's cast, such as Ryu, Ken and Chun-Li.
links.added: A crossover with Marvel's X-Men and two-character tag teams.

links.took: Capcom's Marvel crossover and tag-team fighting.
links.added: A wider Capcom cast like Mega Man and Strider, plus single-use guest assists.
links.extra: Wikipedia says X-Men vs. Street Fighter later became the Marvel vs. Capcom series.

links.took: The Marvel and Capcom crossover and tag-team format.
links.added: Three-on-three teams, assists for every character and a 56-fighter cast.

links.took: Critics point to its three-on-three teams, assists and simplified controls.
links.added: Anime-accurate 3D cel-shading, Dragon Ball's cast and cinematic finishes.
links.extra: Wikipedia says its controls and team mechanics are lifted from Marvel vs. Capcom; producer Tomoko Hiroki said there was no intention to emulate it.

links.took: Arc System Works' presentation, reminiscent of its Guilty Gear Xrd games.
links.added: Dragon Ball characters, three-person teams and destructible stage finishes.

links.took: Daisuke Ishiwatari wanted to make a game like Street Fighter, admiring SF2's simplicity and tactics.
links.added: Flashy, fast fights with rock and metal music and anime-style characters.
links.extra: He later moved away from SF2's simplicity toward a 'flashy game' after talks with programmer Hideyuki Anbe.

links.took: Arc System Works' high-speed 2D fighting from Guilty Gear.
links.added: A new world and cast, each fighter with a unique 'Drive' mechanic.

links.took: Guilty Gear's cast, metal soundtrack and fast fighting.
links.added: 3D models made to look hand-drawn, wall breaks and rollback netcode.
links.extra: Many Guilty Gear games came in between, including the Xrd series.

links.took: Arc System Works' 3D models animated like 2D art.
links.added: Slower, spacing-focused fights and optional one-button special moves.

links.took: Model 1 polygon technology: Virtua Fighter's development began right after Virtua Racing.
links.added: The first fighting game with 3D polygon characters, using guard, punch and kick buttons.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Virtua Racing's technology contributed directly to Virtua Fighter.

links.took: Director Seiichi Ishii, who had designed Virtua Fighter at Sega.
links.added: One button per arm and leg, and a story ending for each fighter.
links.extra: Wikipedia credits Tekken with introducing story modes to fighting games in 1994.

links.took: Texture-mapped polygon graphics similar to Namco's Ridge Racer.
links.added: Texture-mapped 3D fighters on Namco's PlayStation-based System 11 board.

links.took: Virtua Fighter's look and 3D fighting, on the same Model 2 board as Virtua Fighter 2.
links.added: Danger zones in the stage floor and a counter-hold system.
links.extra: Tecmo asked Itagaki for a fighting or racing game similar to Virtua Fighter or Daytona USA.

links.took: Fast 3D polygon action; John Romero cited Virtua Fighter as a major influence on Quake.
links.added: A fully 3D first-person shooter world built from polygons, with online deathmatch.

links.took: Polygon characters: Toby Gard cited Virtua Fighter as an influence on Lara Croft.
links.added: A polygon heroine exploring 3D tombs, with climbing, jumping and puzzles.

links.took: Capcom's six-button 2D fighting series, with Ryu and Ken.
links.added: Parrying, a new cast and detailed animation on the CPS-3 board.

links.took: Street Fighter III's parry system and New Generation cast.
links.added: Chun-Li's return, more fighters and refined balance.
links.extra: Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact (1997) came in between.

links.took: The story and fighters of the first three Mortal Kombat games, retold.
links.added: X-ray moves, a cinematic story mode and a tag-team mode.

links.took: NetherRealm's engine and fighting style from Mortal Kombat (2011).
links.added: DC Comics characters, stage transitions and interactive objects.

links.took: NetherRealm's modern Mortal Kombat formula and cast.
links.added: A rebooted timeline and Kameo assist fighters.
links.extra: Mortal Kombat X and 11 came in between.

links.took: Tekken's four-limb controls and cast, including Jin Kazama.
links.added: The Heat system and rollback netcode.

links.took: Arena fights on moving, multi-level stages with items to grab, per third-party sources.
links.added: Nintendo characters, up to four players and knocking foes off the stage.
links.extra: Third-party sources call The Outfoxies a possible inspiration; Masahiro Sakurai's own account doesn't name it.

links.took: Knockout-based platform fighting, where foes are knocked off the stage.
links.added: Free-to-play, weapon pickups that change each character's moves, and cross-play.
links.extra: Wikipedia lists it among indie games that imitated Smash Bros.' mechanics.

links.took: Smash Bros.' mechanics, including Melee-style wavedashing, rebuilt for speed.
links.added: Faster, more combo-heavy fights with no items or shields, and elemental animal fighters.
links.extra: Wikipedia says the aim was a faster, more combo-oriented game than Super Smash Bros.

links.took: Smash Bros.-style platform fighting with famous characters from many series.
links.added: Two-versus-two team play with Warner Bros. characters, free-to-play.

src.t: Wikipedia: MultiVersus (cites Polygon and GameSpot comparisons)

links.took: Smash Bros.-style platform fighting with a crossover cast.
links.added: Nickelodeon cartoon characters such as SpongeBob and the Ninja Turtles.
